meta.title: Who really said "In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Benjamin Franklin, in a letter of 13 November 1789 — though the saying was already a proverb when he used it. Here is the letter and the older evidence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes'?
meta.ogDescription: Franklin wrote it to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy on 13 November 1789. But ‘death and taxes’ was in print by 1716, and by 1717 Defoe called it a proverb.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Franklin wrote it to the French physicist Jean-Baptiste Le Roy on 13 November 1789, five months before his death. The full sentence is ‘Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.’ It was first printed in The Private Correspondence of Benjamin Franklin, published by his grandson William Temple Franklin in 1817. Franklin did not coin the saying — it was already proverbial — but these are his words.

source.excerpt: Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the sentence from the letter and cites its printing: The Private Correspondence of Benjamin Franklin, Published from the Originals by His Grandson William Temple Franklin, second edition, vol. 1, letter titled ‘On the Affairs of France’, dated 13 November 1789, starting at p. 265 and quoted at p. 266 (London: Henry Colburn, 1817).

Wikipedia’s article on the idiom ↗ quotes the identical wording and attributes it to the 1789 Le Roy letter, citing Jared Sparks, The Writings of Benjamin Franklin, vol. X (1856), p. 410. Two independent transcriptions matching word for word is what makes this ‘verified’ rather than ‘attributed’.
Wikiquote’s Franklin page ↗ carries it in its sourced section with the same date and recipient, and notes the 1817 Private Correspondence printing at p. 266.
The recipient is a real and identifiable correspondent: Jean-Baptiste Le Roy ↗ (1720–1800), a French physicist and a major contributor to Diderot and d’Alembert’s Encyclopédie.
source.excerptNote: The famous half is the clause after the semicolon. Franklin was writing about the new United States Constitution, so the joke is a hedge on a specific thing — whether the new government would last — not a general remark about life.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: About Benjamin Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, publisher of Poor Richard’s Almanack, experimental scientist, and the diplomat who secured the French alliance in the American Revolution. He signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution — which is what makes this letter, written eight months into the new government and five months before he died, worth reading as a verdict rather than a wisecrack.

copyAttribution: "In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes." —Benjamin Franklin, letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, 13 November 1789, first printed in The Private Correspondence of Benjamin Franklin (1817), vol. 1, p. 266. The saying was already proverbial: Christopher Bullock used it in 1716. Provenance verified at quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Franklin said it. He did not invent it.
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Franklin is correct and the wording is his. What is wrong is the widespread belief that he came up with the idea — ‘death and taxes’ was a stock joke in English decades before he wrote that letter.

items.why: In Bullock’s farce The Cobler of Preston, staged and published in 1716, the drunken cobbler Toby Guzzle says ‘’tis impossible to be sure of any thing but Death and Taxes’. Wikipedia’s article on the idiom calls it the earliest known iteration ↗; its article on the play ↗ calls the afterpiece the origin of the phrase. QI quotes the passage ↗ from a verified scan of the 1716 edition, p. 14.

Defoe’s Fair Payment No Spunge (1717) refers to ‘a Proverb or by-Word among us, that there is nothing sure, but Death and Taxes’. That is the strongest single piece of evidence against Franklin as originator: a writer calling it a proverb seventy-two years before Franklin used it see the citation ↗.

items.who: Ward 1724, Defoe 1726, Reed 1769, Bridges 1770, The Gentleman’s Magazine 1783
items.why: QI lists a chain of printed uses running through the eighteenth century before Franklin’s letter. What Franklin’s usage did was make it famous — QI’s own conclusion is that his 1789 letter ‘helped to popularize the expression’ the full chronology ↗.

QI records that Twain appears to have used the expression in an 1884 letter to Frank Fuller — and says plainly that it has not verified that report. Either way it is a century and a half after Bullock, so it is not an origin QI on the Twain report ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Franklin wrote these words on 13 November 1789. Christopher Bullock got the joke into print in 1716, and by 1717 Defoe was already calling it a proverb the full investigation ↗.

context.heading: What he was actually hedging about
lead: The sentence is a judgement on the United States Constitution, which had been in force since 4 March 1789 ↗ — about eight months when Franklin wrote. He tells Le Roy the new government ‘has an appearance that promises permanency’ — and then immediately undercuts himself with the oldest joke about certainty available to him.
He was 83 and had five months to live. The letter went to a friend in a Paris that had stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789 ↗, four months earlier, which is part of why he was writing at all.
context.pull: It is a hedge about one specific thing: whether the new government would last.
